title: Dress for the floor
instruction: Hi-vis vest, safety shoes and safety glasses before you step onto the floor.
rationale: A robot floor is shared with lift trucks and tuggers driven by people, and the hi-vis vest is for their eyes, not the robots' — the robots' scanners see a body either way, but a driver turning a corner needs every bit of contrast they can get.

title: Read the traffic plan
instruction: Find today's lanes, crossings and closed zones before walking onto the floor.
rationale: Robot lanes and crossings change when the floor layout changes, and the traffic plan is what shows today's version — walking the floor from memory means walking yesterday's lanes.

title: Cross at the marked point
instruction: Walk to the marked crossing, look both ways and cross.
rationale: The marked crossing is where robots are configured to slow and where they expect people, and it is the only place where the floor's design has already done half the work of keeping you out of a robot's path.

title: Run the e-stop drill
instruction: Trigger the drill and confirm each robot on the lane has actually stopped.
rationale: An e-stop drill proves the stop works on every unit, not just the one the technician happened to check last month, and a robot that keeps rolling on the drill is found now instead of on the day somebody needs it to stop.

title: Check the unit's scanner field
instruction: Read the scanner field check and commit only in the green band.
rationale: The robot's scanner is the thing that slows and stops it for people, and the field check is what shows it is clean, aligned and seeing the zone the risk assessment says it should, not a smudged window guessing.

title: Take the faulted unit out of the fleet
instruction: At the fleet console, take unit 14 out of the fleet before touching it.
rationale: A faulted robot the controller still counts as available can be handed a new mission at any moment, and taking it out of the fleet at the console is what guarantees it will not start moving while a person is next to it.

title: Close the lane
instruction: Carry the lane barrier to the lane mouth and set it.
rationale: The barrier tells the fleet and every driver on the floor that this lane is closed, so the recovery happens inside a space nothing else is routed through rather than in a gap between moving robots.

title: Push the unit to the bay
instruction: In manual mode, keep the push steady inside the band as the unit rolls to the service bay.
rationale: A robot pushed in manual mode has no drive holding it back, and a steady push inside the band keeps it under your control instead of rolling on its own into a rack or a person's ankles.

title: Find the cause
instruction: Look along the shelf for what took the unit off its lane.
rationale: A robot that faulted once will fault again unless the cause is found, and the floor debris wound into a caster is also a sign the lane itself needs sweeping before the next unit runs over it.

title: Hold the lane closed
instruction: Hold the lane closure on the console while the unit is inspected.
rationale: The lane stays closed on the console for the whole inspection, not only until the barrier is in place, because a fleet that reopens the lane on its own schedule can route a unit into the space you are working in.

title: Return the unit to the fleet
instruction: Return unit 14 to the fleet once the cause is cleared and the scanner checks green.
rationale: A unit rejoins the fleet only after its fault is cleared and its scanner is proven, because putting it back early turns a known fault into an unexpected one somewhere else on the floor.

title: Reopen the lane
instruction: Remove the barrier and reopen the lane on the console.
rationale: Reopening is done deliberately at both the barrier and the console so that the floor and the fleet agree the lane is live again, instead of one thinking it is closed while the other sends robots through it.

title: Walk the lane
instruction: Before you leave, find what makes this lane less safe than the plan says.
rationale: The traffic plan assumes the floor matches it, and a missing mirror at a blind corner is the kind of gap that lets a person and a robot meet with no warning, so it is reported now rather than noticed after a near miss.

title: Log the drill and the recovery
instruction: Log the e-stop results, the fault cause and the missing mirror.
rationale: The fleet log is how a pattern shows up — the same unit faulting, the same corner causing trouble — and a drill and a recovery that are not written down teach the floor nothing.

situation: Another robot has drifted off its lane toward the walkway where a visitor is standing.
instruction: Hit the fleet pause at the console now.
missed: The fleet kept running with a robot off its lane beside a person. A lost robot is paused first and diagnosed second.

situation: A lift truck has turned into the AMR lane you have just closed for the recovery.
instruction: Use the zone access request to hold the lane closed and wave the truck back.
missed: The lift truck came down the closed lane. A closed lane is only closed if everybody driving the floor is kept out of it.

explanation: That hangs a jacket over the robot's scanner to stop it slowing near the bench. A robot that cannot see is a robot that will not stop for the next person, and its safety comes entirely from that scanner.

That cuts across the live lane between two robots. A robot's scanner is set to slow and stop for what it can see, but a person stepping out from behind a rack or another robot may be inside its stopping distance before it sees them.
That pushes the faulted robot by hand while it is still in the fleet. A unit the controller still thinks is available can be given a new mission and start moving under your hands.
That stands on the robot's lift plate to reach the shelf. The lift plate carries loads, not people, and the robot has no way to know a person is riding it when it decides to move.

title: Gown in the posted order
instruction: Booties at the bench line, then hood and mask, then the coverall.
rationale: The gowning order exists so that each layer goes on without dragging the dirt of the last one onto its clean outside surface — booties at the bench line keep street shoes from ever touching the clean side, and the hood goes under the coverall collar so hair and skin stay sealed in.

title: Read the entry card
instruction: Confirm the part, the bench and the ESD rules posted for today's job.
rationale: The entry card is what says which part is in work, which bench it belongs on and whether today's job needs anything beyond the standing rules — walking in without it means handling a sensitive part on assumptions nobody signed off.

title: Pass through the air shower
instruction: Stand through the full air-shower cycle before the inner door opens.
rationale: The air shower strips the loose particles the gowning room could not, and cutting the cycle short carries them straight onto the benches — the inner door waits on the cycle so the cleanest room in the building is never the one a hurry lets the dust into.

title: Test strap and heel straps
instruction: Wrist strap snug on skin, heel straps on both shoes, then stand on the tester plate.
rationale: A wrist strap that is loose on a sleeve, or a heel strap tucked under a bootie, reads as protection and delivers none — the tester is the only thing in the room that proves the path from this person to ground is actually complete today.

title: Go to the grounded mat
instruction: With a PASS at the tester, go to the grounded mat on the bench.
rationale: Only a PASS earns the bench; a FAIL means the strap or the heel straps are not doing their job and the right move is to fix that first, because the damage a charged hand does to a sensitive part is invisible and often shows up only once the part is in service.

title: Check the mat to ground
instruction: Read the mat's ground check and commit only in the green band the site's procedure sets.
rationale: A dissipative mat with a lifted ground cord is just an insulating sheet with a nice colour, and the meter reading is what shows that this particular mat is still bleeding charge away rather than letting it build under the part.

title: Bring the part in its tote
instruction: Carry the shielded tote to the bench and set it beside the mat before it opens.
rationale: The shielded tote is the part's protection everywhere outside the grounded mat, and it only opens once it is sitting on the bench beside the mat — the part never travels across the room naked, however short the walk looks.

title: Transfer the part to the mat
instruction: Keep the part level and low over the mat as it comes out of the tote.
rationale: A part lifted high or swung across the bench is a part passing through charged air and past charged sleeves; keeping it level and low over the mat keeps it inside the one zone this room has made safe for it.

title: Find the charge source
instruction: Look along the shelf for the thing that has no business near a sensitive part.
rationale: Insulating plastics hold charge that no wrist strap can bleed off, because they are not connected to anything — a foam cup or a plain plastic bag near the mat can charge a part by induction without ever touching it.

title: Run the bench ionizer
instruction: Hold the ionizer on while the insulating fixture is neutralised.
rationale: Some things on the bench cannot be grounded because they insulate, and the ionizer is how their charge is neutralised — held through its full cycle, not waved at the fixture for a second on the way to the next task.

title: Sign the traveller
instruction: Record the strap test, the mat check and the handling on the part's traveller.
rationale: The traveller is what the next station and the quality inspector read, and a handling step that is not written down is a handling step nobody can prove was done under control if the part fails later.

title: Repack the part
instruction: Close the shielded lid and label the tote before it leaves the mat.
rationale: The part leaves the mat the same way it arrived, inside closed shielding — an open tote carried to the next station undoes all the control this bench just exercised, one charged sleeve at a time.

title: Check the strap cord
instruction: Before you leave, find the strap cord that should not go back on the rack.
rationale: A damaged cord hung back on the rack becomes somebody else's failed test tomorrow — or worse, a test that passes intermittently — and taking it out of service now is how the next entry starts with a strap that works.

title: Close the entry log
instruction: Log the test result, the handling and the tagged cord before you degown.
rationale: The entry log ties this person's strap test to this part's handling at this time, which is exactly the record anyone investigating a failed part will ask for, and it closes before degowning while the details are still in front of you.

situation: The wrist strap's coiled cord has popped off the bench ground snap mid-transfer — the continuity monitor is chirping.
instruction: Stop the transfer now, before the part moves any further with no path to ground.
missed: The transfer carried on with the strap off the snap. A part handled by an ungrounded technician can take a discharge that leaves no mark and fails it later.

situation: A visitor in street clothes has opened the air-shower door and is stepping into the bay.
instruction: Call the lead so the visitor is stopped and gowned before coming further in.
missed: Nobody stopped the ungowned visitor. Every step they took into the bay undid the gowning everyone else had done.

explanation: That sets the part down on the bare steel of the bench beside the mat. An unprotected part on an ungrounded or insulating surface can take a static discharge it never recovers from, and the damage may not show until the part fails in service.

That pulls the coverall on over street shoes before the booties. Gowning out of order drags the floor's particles up onto the outside of the garment, which is exactly the surface the cleanroom exists to keep clean.
That carries the part out of its shielded tote across the room. Outside the tote and away from the mat, the part is exposed to every charged surface and every particle between the door and the bench.

That walks to the bench without testing the wrist strap and heel straps. A strap that looks fine can have a broken conductor inside it, and a person charged up by walking across the floor discharges into the first part they touch without ever feeling it.

title: Prepare for the bench
instruction: Safety glasses, safety shoes and long hair tied back before the bench.
rationale: Working beside a moving arm means loose hair, sleeves and lanyards are the things that get caught first, and the glasses protect against a part flicked from the gripper, which the arm's own safety functions do nothing about.

title: Open the risk assessment
instruction: Open the application's risk assessment and read the hazards it lists.
rationale: A collaborative application is only collaborative because a risk assessment showed its hazards are controlled for this task, this tool and this layout, and the sheet is where those findings live and where any change has to be written first.

title: Walk the application
instruction: Walk the operator's tasks, then check the gripper and the layout against the sheet.
rationale: The assessment is only valid for the tasks, tool and layout it describes, and walking each against the bench as it stands today is how a changed fixture or a swapped gripper is caught before it becomes the hazard nobody assessed.

title: Check the area scanner
instruction: Check the area scanner's window is clean and unobstructed.
rationale: The area scanner is what the arm relies on to know where people are, and a smudged or obstructed window can make it see a person too late or not at all, which undoes speed-and-separation without any warning on the screen.

title: Prove the zones with a body
instruction: Walk into the warning zone and watch the arm slow, then into the protective zone and watch it stop.
rationale: Speed-and-separation only works if the arm really slows and stops at the zones the assessment set, and the only honest test is a person walking into them while the arm runs, because a settings screen shows intent, not behaviour.

title: Check the stopping performance
instruction: Read the stopping check and commit only in the green band the manual sets.
rationale: The separation distance depends on how quickly the arm actually stops, and a stopping check outside its band means the zones drawn on the floor are too small for the arm as it behaves today.

title: Stage the part
instruction: Carry a part blank to the fixture tray.
rationale: Parts are staged in the tray the assessment describes so that the operator's hands go only where the analysis expected them, rather than into the arm's path to rescue a part set down somewhere convenient.

title: Walk the approach
instruction: Keep your approach to the bench steady inside the band as the arm runs.
rationale: The zones are calibrated for a person walking at a normal pace, and a steady approach inside the band shows the arm slowing smoothly rather than stopping abruptly, which tells you the separation is set right for real use.

title: Find the unassessed hazard
instruction: Look along the shelf for the hazard the sheet does not cover.
rationale: Walking the bench always turns up something the desk review missed, and a sharp corner where the arm can trap a hand is exactly the kind of detail that decides whether contact is harmless or not.

title: Run the contact check
instruction: Hold the contact check through the test the manual describes.
rationale: Where the application relies on limiting contact force, the check is run through its whole cycle with the manufacturer's test method, because a partial check proves nothing about the moment the arm actually meets a hand.

title: Release the bench
instruction: With every control tested, release the bench for use.
rationale: Release is the statement that every hazard on the sheet has a control and every control has been tested, and releasing on anything less is releasing on hope rather than on the evidence the assessment asked for.

title: Update the risk assessment
instruction: Add the sharp corner and its guard to the sheet.
rationale: A hazard found and fixed but not written into the assessment will be missed again the next time the bench is changed, and updating the sheet is how the finding outlives the person who found it.

title: Check the pendant
instruction: Before you leave, find the setting that should not be left as it is.
rationale: A pendant left in the wrong mode is how the next person teaching the arm finds it moving faster than they expect, so it is returned to the state the procedure sets before the bench is left.

title: Sign the release
instruction: Sign the release log with the tests run and the sheet updated.
rationale: The release log records who tested what and when, so that when the bench changes, the next person knows what the last release was based on and what needs testing again.

situation: You have walked into the warning zone and the arm has not slowed at all.
instruction: Hit the cobot e-stop now.
missed: The arm kept full speed with a person in the zone. A failed control is stopped, not watched.

situation: A student at the next desk is reaching into the cobot's work area to pick up a part.
instruction: Call the instructor so the student is stopped and briefed.
missed: Nobody stopped the student reaching into the work area. The bench was never assessed for that person or that task.

explanation: That mutes the area scanner so the arm stops slowing when you lean in. Speed-and-separation is the control; muting it turns a collaborative application into an unguarded robot with a person beside it.
That signs the scanner zones off from the settings screen without walking into them. Settings say what the scanner should do; only a body walking into the zone shows what it actually does.
That raises the arm's speed to hit the cycle time without reassessing. Speed changes the separation the arm needs, and a new speed means a new assessment, not a quicker version of the old one.
That fits the sharp-edged finger set the assessment never covered. The collaborative assessment was done for the gripper on the sheet; a new tool with edges is a new hazard the sheet does not answer.

title: Gown and suit up for the lift
instruction: Cleanroom gown, a bump cap under the hood and rigging gloves over the cleanroom gloves.
rationale: A lift in a cleanroom needs both the room's contamination control and the rigging crew's protection, and wearing rigging gloves over the cleanroom gloves keeps the payload clean while still protecting hands from sling edges and pinch points.

title: Brief the lift plan
instruction: Walk the crew through the lift plan: load, rigging, path, signals and stop.
rationale: The lift plan is where the weight, the rigging, the crane's capacity and the travel path were worked out in advance, and briefing it means every person on the lift knows their job and knows that any of them can call stop.

title: Inspect crane and rigging
instruction: Inspect the sling's tag and body, the hook latch and the pendant functions.
rationale: The pre-use inspection is what catches the sling that was cut on the last lift, the latch that no longer closes and the pendant button that sticks, each of which is invisible until it matters and each of which the lift plan assumed was fine.

title: Name the signal person
instruction: Confirm the one designated signal person before the hook moves.
rationale: One designated signal person means the operator follows one voice, and naming them out loud before the lift removes the confusion that comes from two helpful people giving two different signals.

title: Check the hook is plumb
instruction: Read the plumb check and commit only when the hook is over the load's centre.
rationale: A hook that is not over the load's centre of gravity tilts or swings the payload the moment it leaves the stand, and checking plumb before taking the weight is how that swing is prevented instead of reacted to.

title: Attach the tag line
instruction: Carry the tag line to the payload fixture and clip it on.
rationale: The tag line lets a hand control the payload's rotation from outside the fall zone, which is what keeps people from reaching for a swinging load with their hands.

title: Make the trial lift
instruction: On the signal, lift the payload just clear of the stand and hold.
rationale: The trial lift takes the weight just clear of the stand and holds it, so the rigging, the balance and the hoist brake are proven while the load is only a hand's width off its support, not over the floor.

title: Travel the payload
instruction: Keep the crane's travel inside the band on the signal person's direction.
rationale: Smooth, slow travel is what keeps the payload from swinging, and holding the speed inside the band means the tag-line hands can keep up and the load arrives at the set-down stand under control.

title: Find the damaged rigging
instruction: Look along the rack for the rigging that must not be used again.
rationale: Damaged rigging left on the rack is the next lift's failure, and taking it out of service with a tag now means nobody picks it up in a hurry because it was the nearest one.

title: Lower onto the stand
instruction: Hold the lower control for a slow set-down onto the stand.
rationale: The set-down is where fingers and feet get caught and where a payload can be jolted, and a slow, held lower lets the crew guide it onto the stand without anybody's hand between the load and the support.

title: Confirm the load is supported
instruction: Confirm the payload is fully on the stand before slackening the rigging.
rationale: The rigging is only slackened once the stand is carrying the load, because unhooking a payload that is still partly on the sling can let it shift or tip on the stand.

title: Unrig and clear the hook
instruction: Remove the sling and raise the hook clear.
rationale: The hook is raised clear so nobody walks into it and so the crane can be parked, and the sling comes off by hand only once the load is supported and the operator has stopped.

title: Walk the path
instruction: Before you leave, find what is blocking the next lift's path.
rationale: The next lift's plan will assume the path is clear, and a cart parked in it now is the obstruction that forces a crew to improvise under a suspended load later.

title: Log the lift
instruction: Log the lift, the tagged sling and the path issue.
rationale: The lift log is how the site sees which rigging keeps getting damaged and which paths keep getting blocked, and a lift that is not logged leaves the next plan written on assumptions.

situation: The payload has started to swing toward the cleanroom wall during the travel.
instruction: Call a stop and hit the crane stop now.
missed: The crane kept travelling with the load swinging. A swing is settled by stopping, not by travelling faster to outrun it.

situation: A technician is walking into the travel path under the next leg of the move.
instruction: Have the signal person hold the crane until the path is clear.
missed: Nobody held the crane while a person walked into the path. The next leg would have carried the load over them.

explanation: That drags the payload sideways with the hook off plumb. A side pull swings the load when it leaves the stand and puts forces on the crane it was never meant to take.
That rigs the sling without inspecting it because it was fine last week. Slings are damaged by the lifts between inspections, and a cut or crushed sling looks fine until it is loaded.

That takes a signal from the technician on the far side as well as from the designated signal person. Two voices giving signals is how a crane ends up moving two ways at once; only the stop is anybody's to give.

That walks under the suspended payload to adjust a tag line. Nothing about a lift plan makes it safe to be under a load; rigging, hooks and brakes can all fail, and the person under the load has no time to move.

title: Suit up for the cell
instruction: Safety glasses, safety shoes and cut-resistant gloves before the gate.
rationale: The inside of a robot cell is full of fixtures, sheet edges and parts at hand height, and the gloves and glasses are there for the ordinary cuts and flying clips of clearing a jam, not for the arm, which only isolation protects you from.

title: Read the lockout procedure
instruction: Confirm every energy source the cell's written procedure lists before touching anything.
rationale: A robot cell usually carries more than one energy source — electrical, pneumatic, sometimes a gravity-loaded axis — and the written procedure is what lists them all, so none is missed because it was not the one you were thinking about.

title: Bring the cell to a normal stop
instruction: Use the cycle stop to end the program at a safe point.
rationale: A normal cycle stop parks the arm at the end of its motion instead of freezing it mid-path with a part in the gripper, which is what makes the isolation that follows a controlled one rather than a scramble.

title: Isolate and lock out
instruction: Open the disconnect, hang your own lock and tag, then dump the air.
rationale: Opening the disconnect removes the power, your own lock makes sure only you can restore it, and dumping the air removes the second source that could still close a gripper or push a slide — in that order, so no step relies on one that has not happened yet.

title: Try the start
instruction: Press the cell start to prove it will not run.
rationale: The try-start is the test that turns 'I opened the disconnect' into 'this cell cannot move' — a wrong breaker, a second feed or a bypassed circuit shows up here, harmlessly, instead of when someone is inside.

title: Verify zero energy
instruction: Read the cell's energy check and commit only once it reads zero.
rationale: Stored energy outlives the switch — a capacitor bank, trapped air in a line, a spring-loaded clamp — and the meter reading is what shows that the energy the procedure listed is actually gone rather than merely disconnected.

title: Block the raised axis
instruction: Carry the block to the arm's rest point and seat it under the raised axis.
rationale: An axis held up only by its brake can drop without any power at all, and a mechanical block under it is what makes working beneath the arm safe even if that brake is released or fails.

title: Jog in reduced speed
instruction: With the pendant in reduced speed, keep the jog inside the band while the arm moves clear.
rationale: Teaching or jogging inside the cell is done in the reduced-speed mode the manufacturer's manual sets, with the enabling switch held, so that a person close to the arm always has time to react and a single release stops it.

title: Find the cause
instruction: Look along the shelf for what caused the jam.
rationale: Clearing a jam without finding its cause means the cell will jam again, probably on the next shift, and the frayed cable found now is also a live electrical hazard the moment power comes back.

title: Bleed the trapped air
instruction: Hold the bleed valve open until the line gauge falls to nothing.
rationale: The dump valve empties the supply, but air trapped between a closed valve and a cylinder can still move a clamp when a fitting is loosened, and holding the bleed open is how that last pocket is let out on purpose.

title: Remove the block
instruction: Take the axis block out once the work under the arm is done.
rationale: The block comes out before restart because an arm driven into its own block can damage itself or throw the block, and every tool and block brought into the cell has to come back out with the person who brought it.

title: Clear the cell
instruction: Count everyone out and check the floor for tools before the lock comes off.
rationale: Restoring energy is only safe once every person is outside the fence and nothing is left inside for the arm to hit, and the head count is the one check that makes the first of those a fact.

title: Check the guarding
instruction: Before restart, find the guard that is not doing its job.
rationale: Guards and interlocks are checked before restart, not assumed, because a gate that looks shut but has not made its interlock is a gate that will not stop the arm the next time somebody opens it.

title: Remove your lock and log it
instruction: Remove your own lock, restore energy per the procedure and log the entry.
rationale: The lock comes off only by the hand that put it on, after the head count and the guard check, and the log is what tells the next shift what was done inside their cell and what still needs parts.

situation: The arm has started creeping on its own while the pendant is in your hand.
instruction: Let go of the enabling switch and hit the cell stop now.
missed: The arm kept creeping with a person inside the cell. Unexpected motion is answered with a stop, not watched to see where it goes.

situation: The incoming shift's operator is reaching for the disconnect to restart the cell, not knowing you are still inside.
instruction: Point to your personal lock on the disconnect and stop the restart.
missed: Nobody stopped the restart while you were still in the cell. A lock no one pointed to is a lock the next person may try to work around.

explanation: That hangs a coworker's lock on the disconnect for you. A lock only protects the person who holds its key; if somebody else can take it off, it is protecting them, not you.

That jumpers the gate interlock so the cell keeps running with the gate open. An interlock defeated for convenience is a guard that is not there, and it is the one piece of the cell designed for the day somebody forgets.
That walks under the raised arm without blocking it. An axis held up by its brake can drop when the brake is released or fails, and the arm does not need power to move downward.
That reaches over the light curtain to clear the part with the arm in automatic. A curtain stops the arm when it sees a body break the beam; a hand reaching over the top may never break it at all.

title: Suit up for the test area
instruction: Hearing protection, safety glasses and hi-vis before the sweep.
rationale: A test area is loud even between runs and full of vehicles and cables, and the hi-vis is what lets the conductor pick out every person on the zone camera during the sweep, which is the whole point of sweeping.

title: Read the test procedure
instruction: Confirm the zone distance, the stations on the net and the hold rules.
rationale: The test procedure sets the exclusion zone, lists every station that must give a go and states who may call a hold, and a crew that has not read it is running somebody else's memory of a different test.

title: Sweep the zone on foot
instruction: Walk every sector of the zone, including the lee of the deflector.
rationale: The sweep is done on foot because the places a person is most likely to be missed — behind cabinets, under vehicles, in the lee of the deflector — are exactly the places a window or a camera cannot see into.

title: Chain and post the zone
instruction: Chain the zone entry and hang the DANGER sign.
rationale: The chain and the sign turn the swept zone into a closed one, so that nobody arriving after the sweep walks in unaware, and the sign states the hazard in the standard format every worker is trained to read.

title: Match the head count
instruction: Read the head count against the roster and commit only when it matches.
rationale: A head count that matches the roster is the only evidence that everybody who came into the test area is now in the bunker, and a count that is one short is a reason to stop, not a rounding error.

title: Give your station's go
instruction: With your station ready, give your go on the net.
rationale: Each station's go is a statement that its part of the test is ready and safe, and giving it only when that is true is what makes the poll mean something rather than being a round of habit.

title: Close the bunker shutter
instruction: Carry the shutter to the bunker window and close it.
rationale: The shutter protects the people behind the window from anything the stand might throw if the run goes wrong, and it goes on before the countdown because nobody will have time to fit it during one.

title: Run the countdown poll
instruction: Keep the countdown poll inside the band as each station reports.
rationale: A countdown poll that races skips stations and one that drags invites people to wander, and keeping it in the band means every station is heard and the net stays focused on the one thing that matters: whether to hold.

title: Find the zone issue
instruction: On the camera, find what should not be loose in the zone.
rationale: Anything loose in the zone can move during a run, and a cable left across the path is also what trips the first person walking back out, so it is found on the camera now rather than after.

title: Safe the stand
instruction: Hold the safing switch through the procedure's safing sequence.
rationale: The end of a run is not the end of the hazard; stored energy, hot surfaces and trapped pressure remain until the safing sequence has run, and holding the switch through the whole sequence is what lets the stand reach a state people can approach.

title: Lock out the stand
instruction: Apply the lockout to the stand's control before the zone opens.
rationale: The lockout keeps the stand from being started while people are on the pad, turning the safing into a state nobody can undo by accident from the bunker.

title: Open the zone
instruction: Call the all clear on the net, then lower the chain.
rationale: The all clear on the net is what tells every station the zone is open, and lowering the chain only after it means the physical barrier and the spoken one always agree.

title: Check the signage
instruction: Before you leave, find the sign that no longer does its job.
rationale: Zone signs weather in the sun and the exhaust, and a faded one is replaced now because the next crew will rely on it the same way this one did.

title: Close the test log
instruction: Log the sweep, the count, any holds and the zone issues.
rationale: The test log is the record the next test and any investigation reads, and a hold that is logged with its reason teaches the whole site something, while one that is not is just a delay nobody remembers.

situation: The zone camera shows a person walking in past the chain during the countdown.
instruction: Call a hold now.
missed: The countdown kept running with a person inside the zone. A hold costs minutes; not calling it can cost a life.

situation: A driver has unhooked the zone chain to bring a cart in before the stand is safed.
instruction: Get the zone chain back up before anyone else walks through.
missed: The chain stayed down before the stand was safed. The zone was open to anyone who walked past.

explanation: That starts the countdown with the head count one short because someone probably left early. An unmatched count means a person may be inside the zone, and the countdown waits until the count is a fact.
That signs the sweep off from the bunker window without walking the zone. Somebody kneeling behind a cabinet or a vehicle parked in the lee of the deflector cannot be seen from the window.
That unhooks the zone chain to let a vehicle through during the countdown. The chain is the zone; a gap in it is an invitation to the next person to walk through too.
That walks out to the stand before it has been made safe. The run ending is not the same as the stand holding no energy, and the procedure's safing steps are what make the walk out survivable.

title: Read the setup sheet
instruction: Check the part, the fixture, the tool list, the work offset and the first-article dimensions.
rationale: The setup sheet is the contract between the programmer and the machinist, written by someone who is not standing at this machine. Everything measured, torqued or offset in this job — the fixture, the tool list, the work offset, the tolerance band — is checked against a number on this sheet, not against what looks right.

title: Make the machine safe to approach
instruction: Stop the spindle, take the machine out of auto to manual, then lock and tag.
rationale: A stopped spindle is not a safe spindle while the control can still run a queued program off a cycle-start signal from anywhere on the network. Manual mode takes that queued program out of play, and the lock is what stops a second person from putting it back while a hand is in the envelope.

title: Set the fixture and load the part
instruction: Seat the fixture on a clean table, bolt and locate it, then load the part in the vise.
rationale: Everything downstream — the tool offset, the first article, every part after it — assumes the fixture has not moved since it was located and bolted down. A single chip trapped under a fixture face is a tenth of an inch of tilt that shows up as the same error on every part cut in this run, not just the first one.

title: Torque the workholding
instruction: Bring the vise to the torque on the fixture drawing and commit inside the band.
rationale: Under-clamped, the part rides up under cutting load and comes out of the vise at cutting speed, taking the tool with it. Over-clamped, thin-wall stock distorts under the jaw pressure and springs back the moment the clamp is released, so a part that measured perfectly in the vise is out of tolerance the second it's free.

title: Inspect and load the tool
instruction: Check the insert, the holder and the pull stud, then load the tool into the spindle.
rationale: A cracked insert or a loose pull stud is invisible once the tool is buried in the holder and turning at spindle speed. At that speed either one becomes shrapnel inside a sheet-metal enclosure built to contain chips and coolant, not a piece of tooling that has come apart under load.

title: Take your lock off before anything moves
instruction: Get your hands and your tools out of the envelope, then remove your lock and tag.
rationale: Your lock, your call — nobody takes it off but you, and it comes off only once the envelope is empty. Everything from the tool setter onwards moves the machine, and none of it happens with a lock hanging on it.

title: Measure the tool and set the offset
instruction: Touch the tool off on the setter and commit the length offset inside the band.
rationale: The length offset is the one number that tells the control exactly where the tip of this specific tool sits relative to the part zero. Wrong by a tenth of an inch and the very first programmed move either cuts nothing but air or drives the tool straight through the fixture before anyone can react.

title: Single-block dry run above the part
instruction: Run the program single-block at reduced feed with the tool held clear above the part.
rationale: The dry run is where a wrong offset, a missed clamp or a rapid into the fixture shows up harmlessly. Every setup gets one, every time, and it is held above the part so a mistake costs nothing.

title: Close the door
instruction: Close the enclosure door and confirm the interlock is made before cycle start.
rationale: The enclosure is the guard, not decoration around the machine. Closed and interlocked, it contains a part or a broken tool that comes loose under cutting load; left open, it is simply a window a piece of metal leaves through at whatever speed the spindle was turning when it let go.

title: Run the first part
instruction: Turn the control to auto and start the cycle, staying at the panel through the first part.
rationale: The operator stays at the panel with a hand near feed hold for the whole first part, watching the cut and listening to it, because the first part is the one that finds whatever mistake the dry run couldn't — a clamp that was fine in the air but not under load, an offset that was close enough to pass the touch-off but not the cut.

title: Measure the first article
instruction: Take the critical dimension with the micrometer and commit inside the drawing tolerance.
rationale: The first article is what says the setup makes good parts. Nothing else in the run is measured until this one is signed off, because everything after it is a copy of it.

title: Clear the chips properly
instruction: Take the brush and the chip vacuum to the nest on the table.
rationale: A brush and a vacuum, never air and never a bare hand — chips off a machine still carry the heat of the cut and a stringer wraps around whatever touches it. That single habit, repeated every time without exception, is most of what separates a machinist who keeps all ten fingers from one who doesn't.

title: Walk the machine before the run
instruction: Check the coolant, the covers and the panel, and click anything that will not survive a full run.
rationale: A production run is hours of largely unattended cutting once it's turned loose. Coolant that's marginal now runs dry by the fiftieth part, and a way cover that's split now is packed with swarf and scoring the ways by the hundredth — walked and caught here, either one is a five-minute fix instead of a ruined slide.

situation: A coworker leans in through the open door to point at something on the print, well inside the tool's swept path while the dry run is still moving.
instruction: Somebody's leaning into the envelope while the tool is still sweeping.
missed: Nobody froze it. The head kept travelling its programmed path a foot from a coworker leaning into the envelope to talk — a dry run only proves the program, it does not guarantee the tool stays clear of a person standing where it happens to swing.

situation: The enclosure's air curtain catches the setup sheet and slides it off the bench toward the chip pan, right as you're watching the dry run instead of the bench.
instruction: The setup sheet just blew off the bench.
missed: The sheet sat in the chip pan through the rest of the setup. The first article got measured against a tolerance recalled from memory, and it was the band for the previous revision of this print, not the current one.

explanation: You blew the chips off with the air hose. Compressed air drives a chip through skin and into an eye, throws coolant mist into the air you are breathing, and packs swarf into the ways where it scores them.

You pulled the chip nest off with a bare hand. Machining chips are a continuous razor at the temperature they came off the cut, and a stringer wrapped on a finger takes the finger with it if the spindle moves.

You pressed cycle start with the door open. The interlock is the only thing between the operator and a part that comes out of the vise at cutting speed; defeating it is the classic machine-shop fatality.

You reached into the work envelope with the spindle live. A machining centre restarts on a queued command and a tool at four thousand revolutions does not care what is in the way; the door interlock exists because hands are faster than judgement and slower than a spindle.

title: Read the ticket
instruction: Check the jam location, the drive, and the lockout points for this conveyor.
rationale: One conveyor line can have a head drive, a gravity take-up and an upstream infeed spur, and each one stores or delivers its own energy independently of the others. The ticket's lockout points are the complete list for this line; you do not discover a second drive still running by finding it at the pulley with your hands already inside the guard.

title: Hit the e-stop
instruction: Stop the belt at the nearest e-stop before approaching the jam.
rationale: The e-stop is the immediate stop, not the isolation — it drops the belt now, on a control circuit that a photoeye or a reset button can re-energise the instant the fault clears. It buys the seconds it takes to walk to the disconnect and put a lock on the source; nobody works near the nip with only the e-stop between them and a moving belt.

title: Lock out the drive
instruction: Open the drive disconnect and hang your lock and tag.
rationale: A belt stopped on its e-stop restarts itself the instant the jam sensor sees clear and the controller resets — a stopped belt is not a safe belt, only a belt waiting for permission. Opening the drive disconnect and hanging your own lock and tag on it is the only thing that takes that permission away from the controller and puts it in your hand alone.

title: Release the stored energy
instruction: Back off the gravity take-up until the belt tension is released and hold until it settles.
rationale: A locked-out belt is dead electrically but not mechanically — the gravity take-up still holds the belt in tension exactly the way it did while running, stored in the sag of the belt itself. Free a jam while that tension is still loaded and the belt snaps taut the instant the obstruction lets go, and whatever hand is on it travels with it toward the nip.

title: Try-start
instruction: With the lockout on, press start — nothing should happen.
rationale: The try-start is the only proof that the lock is actually on the disconnect that feeds this belt and not a breaker that looks identical two panels over. A lock on the wrong device holds just as firmly and looks exactly as locked as the right one — the only thing that tells them apart is whether the belt moves when somebody presses start with your lock already on it.

title: Remove the head guard
instruction: Take the head pulley guard off to reach the jam.
rationale: The guard comes off only after the belt is locked, the tension is bled and the try-start has proven the lockout is real — three checks that all have to pass before the one thing standing between a hand and the nip point is removed. It comes off already knowing it goes back on before the lock does, in that order and no other.

title: Clear the jam
instruction: Pull the jammed carton out of the transfer and set it on the reject stand.
rationale: A hand goes anywhere near the nip only because the belt has already been proven unable to move — lockout, bleed and try-start done, in that order, before this step starts. The carton comes out to the reject stand, not back onto the belt, because a jammed carton put back where it jammed the first time jams the same way the moment the line restarts.

title: Refit the head guard
instruction: Guard back on and fastened before anything else.
rationale: The guard goes back on before the lock comes off, every time, with no exception for a quick restart. Reverse that order even once and there is a window, however short, where the nip point is open and the belt has permission to move — and a nip point does not need long to take a hand, only a fraction of a second of that window existing at all.

title: Walk the line for defeated safeguards
instruction: Check the pull-cords, guards and e-stops along the run and click what has been defeated.
rationale: A jam on a line with a working pull-cord ends with somebody yanking a rope and the belt stopping. The same jam on a line where that cord has been tied back to stop it tripping on false alarms ends with the same reach and no stop at all — the walk down the return side, checking every cord and guard by hand, is how a defeated safeguard gets found and fixed before it is needed for real.

title: Reset the belt tension
instruction: Bring the take-up back until the tension indicator is in the run band.
rationale: The take-up was deliberately backed off to bleed the stored tension before the guard came off, and the belt cannot run correctly slack — it slips on the drive pulley under load and tracks sideways off the frame until it rides against a guard or a support leg. Bringing the take-up back into the run band before restart is what makes the belt track straight and grip the drive the way it was designed to.

title: Remove the lock, reset, restart
instruction: Your lock off, e-stop reset, clear the line, start.
rationale: Your lock comes off last, by you, and only after everything upstream and downstream is checked clear by eye — the guard back on, the pull-cord live, the tension reset. The moment the start button is pressed is the moment every one of those checks gets tested at once, on a belt about to move at full speed with people standing around it.

situation: The infeed spur behind you is still running — it's on its own drive, its own lockout, and nobody touched it. Cartons are stacking up against the locked head end and starting to bow the ones you're leaning past.
instruction: That belt was never part of your lockout. Shut it down before the stack reaches you.
missed: The infeed spur ran the whole time you had your hands in the take-up. A queue of cartons kept pressing forward against a jam that was never built to hold that kind of load, and the point where that gives is usually the moment somebody has a hand in the pinch.

situation: Over at the disconnect your lock is hanging loose and the handle's been bumped part of the way back toward ON. Someone on the next line thought this drive was free.
instruction: Your hands are full of a jammed carton and somebody else has your isolation.
missed: The disconnect went the rest of the way back to ON with the guard off and your hand still inside the transfer clearing the jam. The belt was one photoeye signal away from restarting on its own.

explanation: You tied back the pull-cord so it stops tripping. The pull-cord is the only stop a worker on the line can reach; tied back, the next jam takes a hand with it.
You restarted with the head guard still off. A conveyor runs with every guard on, or it does not run — the guard is what makes the nip a place a hand cannot reach.
You reached into the head pulley nip point with the belt live. A belt draws a hand into the pulley faster than you can pull back; the belt is locked and proven dead before anything goes near a nip.
You stepped onto the belt to reach the jam. A belt is not a walkway; a restart, a slip, or the jam letting go puts you into the transfer chute.

title: Read the pre-shift checklist
instruction: Check today's truck, the load-out order and the capacity plate.
rationale: The checklist is the record that the truck was inspected before the shift; the capacity plate is the number every load is measured against.

title: Pre-shift inspection
instruction: Walk the truck: tires, fork heels and tips, mast chains and hoses, horn and lights.
rationale: A forklift with a cracked fork heel or a slack chain fails under the load it lifts, not in the yard. A truck that fails inspection is tagged out, not driven gently.

title: Belt on
instruction: Sit, and fasten the seatbelt before the key turns.
rationale: In a tip-over the overhead guard protects a belted operator. An unbelted one jumps, and the guard lands on them — the single biggest killer of forklift operators.

title: Secure the trailer
instruction: Chock the trailer wheels and engage the dock lock on the rear impact guard — both, before the plate.
rationale: The chock stops creep; the lock stops a driver pulling away. Either one alone is the accident the other would have prevented.

title: Set the dock plate
instruction: Bring the dock plate down and seat its lip on the trailer bed.
rationale: The plate bridges the gap and the height difference. It sits on the trailer bed by at least four inches of lip, on a trailer that cannot move.

title: Check the trailer floor and nose
instruction: Look down the trailer: floor sound, nose supported, lights on.
rationale: A trailer floor rots from the inside. The truck weighs three times the load; a soft floor lets it through, and a dropped trailer with no landing-gear support noses down with the truck inside.

title: Check the load against the plate
instruction: Read the pallet weight and load centre against the capacity plate — commit when it is inside the rating.
rationale: The plate rates the truck at a 24-inch load centre. A long pallet moves the centre out and the rating down; the pallet that is 'about right' is the one that tips.

title: Pick the load
instruction: Forks fully under to the heel, mast tilted back, then raise only to travel height — four to six inches.
rationale: Under to the heel so the load cannot slide; back so it rests against the carriage; low so the centre of gravity stays inside the wheelbase.

title: Travel to the trailer
instruction: Hold a steady walking-pace speed, horn at the door, load low and back.
rationale: A forklift stops in its own length only at walking pace. The horn at every door and aisle end is the pedestrian's only warning.

title: Take the ramp in reverse
instruction: Loaded, descend the yard ramp in reverse — load uphill, looking over your shoulder.
rationale: Loaded, the load faces uphill: forward up, reverse down. That keeps the weight over the drive axle and the load against the carriage instead of sliding off the tips.

title: Set the forks to the rack beam
instruction: Stopped at the rack, mast vertical, raise until the forks clear the beam — commit inside the band.
rationale: Two inches over the beam clears it; a foot over is a load that drops onto the beam and a pallet that breaks. The height is set stopped, never while the truck is moving.

title: Walk the dock before the next load
instruction: Look at the plate, the chock and the lock, and click what has moved.
rationale: Every entry pushes the trailer. The dock is checked between loads, not at the end of the shift.

situation: The trailer has walked forward off the plate. There is daylight opening at the dock lip behind you and you are standing in the box.
instruction: Get the trailer locked to the building again.
missed: The gap kept opening while you worked. Trailer separation puts the plate into the gap and the truck four feet down onto the yard, upside down, with the operator underneath it — it is the single most common way a dock kills somebody.

situation: A picker has stepped out of the racking into your aisle, on your blind side behind the load.
instruction: Warn them before you are any closer.
missed: You kept travelling with somebody in the aisle behind the load. Pedestrians struck by forklifts are almost never seen first by the operator — that is the point of the horn at every blind corner, not just the ones with a mirror.

explanation: You drove into a trailer that was not chocked or dock-locked. A trailer creeps a few inches every time a truck enters; a driver hooks up and pulls away with you inside; the plate drops and the truck goes four feet to the yard.
You drove forward down the ramp with a load. On a grade the load points downhill and the truck tips over the front axle; loaded, you go up forward and down in reverse.

You let a coworker ride on the forks. A forklift has one seat and one belt; a person on the forks has neither, and the mast, the load and the overhead guard are all built on the assumption nobody is there.
You walked under the raised load. Forks fail, chains stretch, pallets break — nothing that is lifted is ever stood under, and nothing raised is left unattended.

title: Take the bin entry permit and the fumigation record
instruction: Read what is in the bin, how it is bridged, what was last put on it and when.
rationale: The permit certifies that the entry conditions have been met before anybody goes in. The fumigation record is the half of it that gets forgotten: a treated bin has a re-entry interval on it, and phosphine gives no useful warning at the concentrations that matter.

title: Lock out everything that moves grain
instruction: Open the disconnects for the sweep and the reclaim, lock and tag each one, then try to start them.
rationale: This is the control that matters most in a grain bin, and it is first for a reason: grain only engulfs somebody when it is moving, and what moves it is a motor. Opening the disconnect stops the motor, the lock stops the hand, and the try-to-start is the only part of it that proves you locked the right one.

title: Vacuum the dust off the deck and the ledges
instruction: Hold the wand and keep the suction in the band, working the ledges before the hatch comes off.
rationale: A grain elevator is a dust explosion environment and the grain handling standard requires a housekeeping programme for exactly this reason. Dust lying on a ledge is a nuisance; the same dust airborne is a fuel. It comes down at a rate that lifts it into the hose rather than off the ledge, and it comes down before the bin is opened rather than after.

title: Bond the vacuum and the drop light to the bin steel
instruction: Clamp the bonding lead onto bare metal on the bin before anything electrical goes near the opening.
rationale: Moving grain and moving dust both build static, and a vacuum hose is a machine for generating it. Bonding ties everything to one potential so the charge has somewhere to go that is not a spark across a gap with dust in it.

title: Undog the roof hatch
instruction: Back the dogs off a turn and a half each and lift the cover clear of the coaming.
rationale: The hatch is opened after the isolation and the housekeeping, not before. From the moment it is off, the bin is an open hole in a walking surface and everything that follows happens beside it.

title: Test the air in the headspace and down the manway
instruction: Lower the meter through the opening and commit when the reading is inside the entry band.
rationale: Spoiling grain consumes oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide, so the air over a crusted surface can be well short of breathable while the bin looks entirely ordinary, and fumigant residue sits in the same space. This is not what kills most of the people who die in bins, but it is what kills the ones who never reach the grain.

title: Sound the surface from the opening
instruction: Reach the pole in from the coaming and hold it on the crust while you feel for what is underneath.
rationale: A bridge looks like a floor. The pole is how you find out whether it is one: a crust that gives, drums hollow, or lets the pole straight through has a void under it, and the depth of that void is how far a person would fall before the grain came in on top of them. It is done from the opening, on your knees, with no weight on the grain.

title: Read the crusted wall and set the work position clear of it
instruction: Mark the vertical face of caked grain on the sheet and plan to work above it and to one side.
rationale: A wall of crusted grain is a different hazard from a bridge and carries the opposite rule. A bridge fails under you; a wall fails onto you, in slabs, with a person's weight of grain in every square metre of face. You break it down from above and from the side, and you are never standing under it when it lets go.

title: Rig the harness, the lifeline and the retrieval
instruction: Harness on, lifeline onto the anchor over the hatch, then wind the slack out at the winch.
rationale: The harness and lifeline are what the standard asks for; the slack is the part crews leave out. A line with two metres of slack in it lets an entrant go two metres into the grain before it does anything at all, and two metres is already past saving. Wound tight, the line is a limit on how far you can sink rather than a way of pulling you out afterwards — because nothing pulls you out afterwards.

title: Post the observer and give them a way to call for help
instruction: Observer outside the opening, radio tested in both directions, alarm pull where they can hit it without walking away.
rationale: The observer is required to stay outside the bin and to keep communications going, and the one thing that must never happen is that they leave the hatch to fetch help. So the means of summoning it is at the hatch: a pull station, a radio to the control room, a phone on the platform — anything that raises the plant without costing the entrant the only person watching them.

title: Stage the bin rescue tube at the opening
instruction: Carry the rescue tube across from the platform to the marked spot beside the hatch.
rationale: Rescue equipment suited to the structure is part of the entry, not part of the response. A bin rescue tube is a coffer dam the observer can drop around a partly buried entrant to hold the grain off them while it is augered clear — and it is only any use if it is already beside the hatch, because there is no time to go and look for one.

title: Come down the line to the working position
instruction: Take your weight on the line and come down at a controlled rate, staying off the surface.
rationale: You come down on the line rather than the ladder because the line is the thing holding you, and at a rate the winch can follow. The working position is above the crust and clear of the wall face, with your feet on nothing that could start flowing.

title: Break the bridge from above with the bar
instruction: Work the bar down through the crust from where you are hanging, and hold the work until it gives.
rationale: The bridge is broken with a tool, at arm's length, from above it — the entrant's weight never goes on the grain and never gets below it. When the crust goes it goes all at once and the surface drops several feet in a second, and that exact moment is why the line is tight and why the observer is at the hatch.

title: Read the air again now the void is open
instruction: Second reading, same meter, now that what was under the bridge is in the bin with you.
rationale: The void under a bridge has been sealed beneath spoiling grain for weeks. Breaking the crust vents all of it into the space at once, so the reading that justified the entry describes a bin that no longer exists. You are inside it when this happens, which is why the meter stays on you.

title: Walk the bin and the gallery before you sign it off
instruction: Before the locks come off, look over the sweep, the guards and the ledges; click what needs a work order.
rationale: The bin is the only part of this job with a permit on it, and it is not the part that will hurt the next person. What gets the next crew is the guard nobody refitted and the dust nobody can reach, and both of those are found by somebody walking the plant with their eyes open.

situation: The distributor has swung the fill spout over this bin and the gate lamp above the hatch has gone green. The house is loading out.
instruction: Something upstairs is about to start putting grain in on top of you.
missed: The spout stayed lined up on this bin. The route ran, and the first the crew knew of it was grain coming through the hatch onto the line — which puts a load on an entrant that no harness is rated for, from a direction the observer can do nothing about. The bin was filling while somebody was hanging in it.

situation: The surface under you has started to move. The reclaim is running — somebody has put a lock back in the box and called the bin from the control room.
instruction: The grain is flowing and you are hanging above it.
missed: The reclaim kept running. The crust you had just broken went down the draw cone and took the working position with it, and the line — tight, which is the only reason any of this is survivable — was carrying a load it was never meant to hold against flowing grain. Everyone who has ever been pulled out of this was pulled out because the machinery stopped first.

explanation: You reached for the air hose to blow the dust off the ledges. Compressed air takes a settled layer that was merely dirty and puts it into the air as a suspended cloud, which is the one condition a grain dust deflagration needs and cannot get from dust lying still. Dust comes down by vacuum or by hand, never on an air jet.

You sent the observer in. Now nobody is at the hatch, nobody is tending the line and nobody is left to call the plant — and the observer exists in the standard precisely so that the second person does not become the second casualty. More than one bin fatality has been a would-be rescuer who went in after the first.

You started the sweep auger to help the grain move while somebody was in the bin. Flowing grain takes a person under in seconds — faster than the observer can shout and far faster than anyone can pull them back — and an unguarded sweep will take a leg off on its own account. Nothing that moves grain runs while the bin is occupied.

You put yourself under the vertical face of crusted grain on the wall. That face is tonnes of caked material standing on nothing but its bond to the sheet, and it comes away in slabs with no warning at all. The rule for a wall is the opposite of the rule for a bridge: you work it from above and from the side, never from beneath it.

You took an ordinary shop light into the bin. In a space with grain dust in it the lamp, the switch and the trailing cord are all ignition sources, and the only fitting that belongs in there is one built and rated for a dust atmosphere. Anything else stays out on the deck.

You stepped out onto the crust. A bridge is a shell over a hole, and the moment it gives there is nothing under your feet but the drop and the grain that comes down after you. Walking on grain to make it flow is prohibited outright by the grain handling standard, and it is the practice behind entrapment after entrapment.

title: Suit up before approaching the sorter
instruction: Safety glasses and hearing protection before stepping up to the sorter.
rationale: A flat sorter runs loud enough over a full shift to matter for hearing, and a jammed envelope can flick a sharp paper edge or a staple hard enough to reach an eye — both are covered before a hand goes anywhere near the machine.

title: Read the isolation permit
instruction: Confirm today's LOTO permit for this sorter before touching anything on it.
rationale: The permit is what tells a clerk which disconnect actually isolates this sorter and who else may already be locked onto it — clearing a jam without reading it first means guessing at a disconnect that might belong to an entirely different machine.

title: Read the sorter for what is already wrong with it
instruction: Look over the sorter before touching it. Two things are already wrong with it — find them.
rationale: A sorter that looks fine from the aisle is not the same thing as one a clerk has actually checked — a taped interlock or a missing panel each quietly removes a control the machine depends on, and finding them now costs a work order instead of costing someone the moment the guard door opens on a running machine.

title: Isolate and lock the sorter
instruction: Isolate the sorter at its disconnect, apply your own lock, then apply the tag — in that order.
rationale: The disconnect alone can be closed again by anyone who does not know a hand is about to be inside the guard; the lock is what makes that impossible without that person's own key, and the tag is what tells the next clerk on the floor why the lock is there — skip any one of the three and the jam gets cleared on a promise instead of a proof.

title: Check for residual motion
instruction: Read the sorter's residual motion indicator and commit only once it shows fully stopped.
rationale: A sweep arm that has just been isolated can still be coasting down under its own momentum, and opening the guard on the assumption that isolated means stopped is exactly the gap a residual motion check exists to close — the indicator is the only honest answer, not how quiet the machine sounds.

title: Open the interlocked guard door
instruction: Turn the guard door latch to open it, now that the sorter is isolated and stopped.
rationale: The guard door is the last thing between a hand and the sweep arm's own pinch point, and opening it only after the sorter is proven isolated and stopped is what keeps this step from ever being the moment the machine was still live.

title: Clear the jammed flat
instruction: Carry the jammed flat clear of the feed rollers to the reject tray.
rationale: Clearing the flat with the sorter isolated and the guard open means a hand never has to trust the machine's own restart timer while it is inside the pinch point — the flat comes free because a hand pulled it, not because the sweep arm happened to still be stopped when it did.

title: Inspect the sweep arm and read for shortcuts
instruction: Check the sweep arm the jam was wedged against, and read for two more things already wrong nearby.
rationale: A sweep arm that was scored or bent by the jam will keep snagging the next flat that crosses it, and a tag with no lock or a worn reach-in path are both the kind of shortcut that looks like nothing until the day it is the reason someone's hand was where the sweep arm closed.

title: Close and latch the guard door
instruction: Turn the guard door latch closed and confirm it seats before restoring power.
rationale: A guard door that is not actually latched is not a guard once the sorter is re-energised — confirming the latch now is what keeps this from being the jam that gets cleared safely and then reopened by the first vibration once the machine is running again.

title: Return the isolation
instruction: Remove the tag, remove your lock, then notify the crew — in that order, before the sorter is re-energised.
rationale: The tag and the lock come off in the order they went on, and notifying the crew before restoring power is what keeps anyone else on the floor from being surprised by a sorter that starts moving again — reversing this order is how somebody re-energises a machine while another clerk still believes it is locked out.

title: Prove the interlock before trusting it
instruction: Hold the guard door ajar and confirm the power indicator drops before letting it swing shut again.
rationale: An interlock that was taped over once is an interlock worth proving rather than assuming fixed — holding the door ajar and watching for the power to actually drop is the difference between an interlock that is trusted because it was repaired and one that is trusted because nobody checked.

title: Bring the sorter back up to speed
instruction: Restart the sorter while keeping the induction belt's tracking indicator inside the centred band.
rationale: Watching the tracking indicator through the restart is what catches a belt that is about to walk off true before it starts grinding against the frame — bringing a sorter back to speed is not just a power switch, it is confirming the belt is actually running where it is supposed to.

title: Log the jam, the defects and the fix
instruction: Log the jam, the interlock repair, the missing panel, and the restart before moving on.
rationale: The maintenance log is what turns one cleared jam and one taped-over interlock into a pattern the plant's own maintenance team can actually see — found but never logged is a recurring guarding failure nobody upstream ever gets the chance to fix for good.

situation: Flats are backing up against the induction belt's own guard as the upstream feed keeps running into the paused sorter.
instruction: Signal the upstream operator to pause the feed rather than reaching in to clear the backup by hand.
missed: The backup was reached into instead of signalled upstream. The induction belt feeding it was never isolated by anything this station did to the sorter — it kept running the whole time.

situation: A floor sweeper has started crossing directly in front of the sorter's discharge chute just as the restart begins.
instruction: Call out to the sweeper and hold the restart until they are clear of the chute.
missed: The restart continued with the sweeper still crossing the chute. A discharge chute at running speed does not pause for someone who has not been told to look up.

explanation: The guard door's own safety interlock has been taped over instead of left to do its job. A taped interlock is a door that can open on a running sorter with nothing at all stopping the sweep arm — the whole reason an interlocked guard exists is defeated by a strip of tape nobody ever needs to touch again.

A side access panel has been left off entirely, leaving the induction belt's own pulleys exposed at hand height. A panel that is not there is not a maintenance shortcut — it is a nip point with nothing at all between it and whoever walks past.

That is the shortcut habit of reaching straight into the sweep arm's own pinch point to free a stuck flat by hand instead of isolating the machine first. The sweep arm does not know the difference between a jammed envelope and the fingers pulling it loose, and it closes on either one exactly the same way.

That disconnect carries a danger tag with no personal lock behind it. A tag with nothing locked is only a note somebody left — anyone can close that disconnect back up without ever knowing a hand might be inside the guard, because nothing is actually stopping them.

title: Suit up before the forklift inspection
instruction: Hi-vis vest and hard hat before stepping onto the dock floor.
rationale: A dock floor mixes forklifts, foot traffic and overhead container handling, and the vest and hard hat are what make a handler visible to an operator and protected from whatever might come off a raised load.

title: Read the daily inspection checklist
instruction: Read the forklift's own daily inspection checklist before walking around it.
rationale: The checklist is what turns a walk-around from a glance into an actual inspection — it names the exact points a forklift fails at most often, and reading it first means nothing on that list gets skipped because it did not come to mind unprompted.

title: Walk around the forklift before mounting it
instruction: Walk the truck cold before climbing on. Two things are already wrong with it — find them.
rationale: A forklift that looks fine parked in its row is not the same as one an operator has actually inspected — a missing belt or a cracked fork both look like nothing from a few feet away, and finding them now costs a work order instead of costing a tip-over or a snapped fork under load.

title: Mount up and belt in
instruction: Mount the seat, then fasten the seatbelt — in that order, before touching a single control.
rationale: The belt only does its job if it is fastened before the truck ever moves, not reached for after the first turn already feels a little off — a counterbalance forklift's own stability depends on the operator staying inside the overhead guard exactly where the belt keeps them.

title: Test the horn before moving
instruction: Sound the horn once before the forklift's first move of the shift.
rationale: A dock floor is loud and full of blind corners, and the horn is the one warning a pedestrian or another operator gets before a loaded truck arrives — testing it now is how a dead horn gets found in the yard, not at the one blind corner where it was actually needed.

title: Check the load against the capacity plate
instruction: Read the forklift's own rated capacity plate and commit once the container's load is confirmed within it.
rationale: A forklift's capacity plate is rated for a specific load at a specific fork height, not a general sense of 'this looks liftable' — reading it against what is actually on the forks is what keeps a stable-looking lift from turning into a front-end tip the moment the mast comes up.

title: Read the dock before crossing it
instruction: Look over the dock before the forklift crosses it. Two things are already wrong with it — find them.
rationale: A dock that looks like a normal shift in progress can still be hiding a pedestrian about to walk into the travel path or a trailer nobody has actually restrained yet — both are invisible from a glance and both are exactly what a forklift's own approach can turn into a real injury if they go unnoticed.

title: Engage the trailer restraint
instruction: Turn the restraint control to engage the arm and confirm the green light before crossing the dock plate.
rationale: A trailer that can creep away from the dock opens a gap under the wheels of anything that crosses onto it — the restraint arm is what keeps that trailer physically pinned in place for as long as a forklift needs to be on or off it.

title: Lift and travel the container
instruction: Lift the container clear of the stack and carry it across the dock to the trailer.
rationale: A load lifted low and travelled steadily is a load the operator can see around and stop quickly if the path ahead changes; a load raised high just to clear the stack turns the same short travel into a rolling blind spot for anyone crossing in front of it.

title: Set the load down under control
instruction: Hold the lower control until the container is fully seated, watching the descent the whole way down.
rationale: A load dropped the last few inches rather than set down slowly can shift, tip or crush whatever is under it, and holding the lower control through the full descent — rather than letting go once it looks close enough — is what keeps the set-down controlled instead of merely quick.

title: Check in with the spotter
instruction: Confirm with the spotter that the load is seated and the trailer is clear before backing off the dock plate.
rationale: A spotter sees the trailer's own blind corners from a position the operator cannot, and checking in before backing off the dock plate is what turns 'it looked clear from the seat' into an actual confirmation from someone who could see the whole picture.

title: Log the inspection and the load
instruction: Log the forklift defects found, the load moved, and the dock hazards cleared before the shift closes.
rationale: The log is what turns one cracked fork and one unchocked trailer into a pattern the plant's own safety committee can actually see — found and fixed but never logged is a recurring problem nobody upstream ever gets the chance to solve for good.

situation: A mail handler on foot has stepped into the forklift's own travel path just ahead, carrying a tote and not looking up.
instruction: Sound the horn and hold the truck rather than continuing to travel with a pedestrian in the path.
missed: The forklift kept moving with a pedestrian already in the path. A mast-high load blocks the operator's own forward view at exactly the moment it matters most, and the horn is the only warning a distracted pedestrian gets.

situation: A second forklift is approaching the same dock from the blind side of the container stack, on a converging path.
instruction: Call out over the radio before either truck commits to the corner.
missed: Neither truck called out before the corner. Two forklifts on a blind converging path find out about each other at the corner itself, which is the worst possible place to find out.

explanation: The left fork tine has a visible crack near its heel, right where the load stress actually concentrates. A cracked fork can fail under a load it looks perfectly capable of carrying, and there is no way to tell how much life it has left in it just by looking twice.

This forklift's seatbelt is missing from its mount entirely, not just unfastened. A counterbalance forklift can tip, and the belt is what keeps an operator inside the overhead guard's own protection rather than being thrown clear of it and landing under the truck as it comes down.

A mail handler on foot is walking directly through the forklift's own travel path, carrying totes and looking at them rather than at the truck. A pedestrian in a forklift's path is invisible to the operator the moment they are behind the mast, and the operator is the one who has to notice first.
