instruction: Sign the pull log before moving on to the next task.
rationale: The signed log is the record that this specific pallet, pulled on this specific rotation tag, actually followed the room's own procedure — not assumed fine because it usually does, and not reconstructed from memory once the pallet is already three aisles away on a forklift.

situation: A temperature alarm sounds — the room ran warmer than it should have during an earlier cycle, a sign the door did not seal properly last time.
instruction: Report the alarm to the refrigeration technician rather than continuing the pull as if the room is reading normally.
missed: The alarm was left unreported. A door that has already failed to seal once will fail again, and each time is a longer temperature excursion than the last.

situation: The buddy check-in radio call has gone unanswered.
instruction: Exit the cold room and account for your buddy in person rather than continuing to work alone past the check-in.
missed: The missed check-in was ignored and work continued. A buddy system that gets overridden by feeling fine is not a buddy system any more.

explanation: That door is propped open with a pallet. A cold room held open is a cold room that is not actually cold any more, and it is also a room whose self-closing door — the one thing that limits how long anyone is exposed on a quick errand — has been disabled by the same prop.

That ice patch has built up right at the doorway threshold, exactly where the temperature swings most on every entry and exit. Ice at a threshold is not a surprise anywhere it forms — it is a slip waiting on whoever assumes the floor is as dry as the aisle behind them.

That sign reads 'enter alone' taped over the buddy-system reminder. A buddy system exists for exactly the scenario it looks least necessary in — a quick, familiar errand into a room where nothing has ever gone wrong before is precisely when nobody thinks to miss an associate who does not come back out on time.

That strip curtain has a torn panel hanging loose. A gap in the curtain is a steady stream of warm, humid air finding its way in, and everything that air is carrying condenses and freezes on the first cold surface it reaches — usually the floor, right where somebody is about to walk.

title: Suit up before approaching the line
instruction: Hi-vis vest and safety glasses before stepping up to the conveyor.
rationale: The line runs cartons and stretch-wrapped loads past head height in places, and the glasses are what keeps a dropped strap end or a kicked-up sliver of packing tape out of an eye while both hands are busy with the jam.

title: Read the isolation permit
instruction: Confirm today's LOTO permit for this line before touching anything on it.
rationale: The permit is what tells an associate which disconnect actually isolates this section of line and who else may already be locked onto it — clearing a jam without reading it first means guessing at a disconnect that might belong to a completely different span of conveyor.

title: Read the line for what is already wrong with it
instruction: Look over the line before touching it. Three things are already wrong with it — find them.
rationale: A line that looks fine from the aisle is not the same thing as one an associate has actually checked — a tied-off cord, a propped guard or a reach-in shortcut each quietly removes a control the line depends on, and finding them now costs a work order instead of costing someone the moment the belt restarts on its own.

title: Pull the local E-stop
instruction: Pull the local E-stop cord before reaching anywhere near the jam.
rationale: The pull-cord is the fastest stop this line has, reachable from right where the jam actually is — trying it first, before the slower walk to isolate and lock the drive, is what keeps the belt from moving again the instant a hand gets close to the jam.

title: Isolate and lock the drive
instruction: Isolate the drive at its disconnect, apply your own lock, then apply the tag — in that order.
rationale: The disconnect alone can be closed again by anyone who does not know a hand is about to be inside the guard; the lock is what makes that impossible without that person's own key, and the tag is what tells the next associate walking the line why the lock is there — skip any one of the three and the jam gets cleared on a promise instead of a proof.

title: Check for residual motion
instruction: Read the drive's residual motion indicator and commit only once it shows fully stopped.
rationale: A drive that has just been isolated can still be coasting down under its own momentum, and reaching into the guard on the assumption that isolated means stopped is exactly the gap a residual motion check exists to close — the indicator is the only honest answer, not how quiet the belt sounds.

title: Open the nip-point guard
instruction: Turn the guard latch to open it, now that the drive is isolated and stopped.
rationale: The guard is the last thing between a hand and the nip point, and opening it only after the drive is proven isolated and stopped is what keeps this step from ever being the moment the line was still live.

title: Clear the jam
instruction: Carry the jammed carton clear of the rollers to the reject bin.
rationale: Clearing the carton with the drive isolated and the guard open means a hand never has to trust the line's own restart timer while it is inside the nip point — the carton comes free because a hand pulled it, not because the belt happened to still be stopped when it did.

title: Inspect the rollers
instruction: Check the rollers the jam was wedged against for damage before closing the guard.
rationale: A roller that was scored or dented by the jam will keep snagging the next carton that crosses it — catching that now is a roller swap on a scheduled repair ticket, not a second jam an hour into the next shift.

title: Close and latch the guard
instruction: Turn the guard latch closed and confirm it seats before restoring power.
rationale: A guard that is not actually latched is not a guard once the drive is re-energised — confirming the latch now is what keeps this from being the jam that gets cleared safely and then reopened by the first vibration once the belt is running again.

title: Return the isolation
instruction: Remove the tag, remove your lock, then notify the crew — in that order, before the drive is re-energised.
rationale: The tag and the lock come off in the order they went on, and notifying the crew before restoring power is what keeps anyone else on the line from being surprised by a belt that starts moving again — reversing this order is how somebody re-energises a drive while another associate still believes it is locked out.

title: Bring the line back up to speed
instruction: Restart the drive while keeping the belt tracking indicator inside the centred band.
rationale: Watching the tracking indicator through the restart is what catches a belt that is about to walk off true before it starts grinding against the frame — bringing a conveyor back to speed is not just a power switch, it is confirming the belt is actually running where it is supposed to.

title: Log the jam and the restart
instruction: Log the jam, the isolation and the restart before moving on to the next task.
rationale: The maintenance log is what turns one cleared jam into a pattern a mechanic can actually see — a jam that gets cleared but never logged is a recurring roller problem that nobody upstream ever gets the chance to fix.

situation: The belt has visibly drifted off-centre on the return roller mid-restart, rubbing against the frame.
instruction: Stop the restart and call it in to the mechanic rather than nudging the belt back by hand while it runs.
missed: The drifting belt was left to run. A belt rubbing the frame wears through a cover fast, and the habit of nudging it back by hand is how a caught-in injury actually starts.

situation: A second carton has jammed at the transfer point further down the line while the first is still being cleared.
instruction: Report the second jam to the line lead. Do not reach into it until it has its own isolation.
missed: The second jam was reached into without its own isolation. One locked-out point does not make the next pinch point down the line safe to reach into.

explanation: That nip-point guard is propped open with a block of wood instead of latched — someone left themselves a shortcut back into the pinch point instead of relatching it. A guard that is not actually closed is not actually a guard; it is a suggestion the next pair of hands past it has no reason to notice.

That is the shortcut habit of reaching straight into a running nip point to walk a jam free by hand instead of stopping the line first. A roller does not know the difference between a jammed carton and the fingers pulling it loose, and it will draw either one in exactly the same way once contact is made.

That is the quick-restart lever that skips isolating and locking the drive before the guard opens. A drive that looks stopped because the belt is not moving right now can still restart on its own control logic the moment something downstream calls for product — the isolator and the lock are what make 'stopped' provable instead of hoped for.

That pull-cord is zip-tied off to the frame, out of reach of anyone who actually needs to stop this line in a hurry. A pull-cord that cannot be pulled is a line that only stops when somebody reaches the panel across the room — every second between those two things is a second the belt keeps running over whatever just got caught in it.

title: Suit up before stepping onto the dock
instruction: Hi-vis vest and hard hat before approaching the dock door.
rationale: A dock door is where a forklift, a trailer and foot traffic all share the same few metres, and the vest is what makes an associate visible to a driver whose mirrors do not cover the space directly behind the trailer.

title: Read the dock assignment and paperwork
instruction: Confirm today's dock assignment and the trailer's paperwork before approaching it.
rationale: The dock board is what confirms this is actually the trailer assigned to this door — crossing onto the wrong trailer because it happened to be backed in when the shift started is how a load ends up on the wrong route entirely.

title: Read the dock for what is already wrong with it
instruction: Look the dock over before anything crosses it. Three things are already wrong with it — find them.
rationale: A dock that looks routine from the aisle is not the same thing as one an associate has actually checked — a gap at the bumpers, an unengaged restraint or a taped light each quietly removes a control the crossing depends on, and finding them now costs a callback to the driver instead of costing someone the moment a trailer moves under a loaded forklift.

title: Confirm with the driver
instruction: Confirm with the driver that the trailer's own parking brake is set and the trailer is in gear or blocked.
rationale: The restraint arm and the chocks back up the trailer's own brake — they were never designed to be the only thing holding it, so confirming the brake is actually set is the first control, not a formality before the real ones.

title: Engage the ICC bar restraint
instruction: Turn the restraint control to hook the arm under the trailer's ICC bar.
rationale: The restraint arm is what keeps the trailer from pulling away from the dock while a forklift is on the leveler — engaging it now, before any crossing, is what turns a trailer that happens to be sitting still into one that is actually held.

title: Chock the trailer wheels
instruction: Carry the wheel chocks to the trailer's rear wheels as the restraint's own backup.
rationale: The chocks are what the restraint arm depends on when the ICC bar's own condition is anything less than perfect — carrying them into place now is what keeps a bent or worn bar from being the only thing between this trailer and the dock.

title: Confirm the dock light
instruction: Confirm the dock light reads green — engaged — before anything crosses.
rationale: The dock light is the one signal visible to every forklift operator approaching the door, and reading it honestly, after the tape hazard was already dealt with, is what makes it worth trusting instead of just another light on the wall.

title: Check the leveler's deck angle
instruction: Read the leveler's deck-angle gauge and commit only inside the safe crossing range.
rationale: A leveler extended at too steep an angle changes how a loaded forklift handles the instant its wheels cross onto it — the gauge is the only honest read of that angle, not how level the lip happens to look from the dock.

title: Extend the leveler
instruction: Hold the leveler control until the lip fully seats on the trailer bed.
rationale: Holding the control the whole way through the extension, rather than bumping it in short presses, is what lets the lip find its seat smoothly on the trailer bed instead of dropping the last few centimetres onto it under its own weight.

title: Cross the leveler
instruction: Drive the forklift across while keeping the crossing speed indicator inside the safe band.
rationale: Crossing a leveler too fast bounces a loaded fork exactly where the gap between the dock and the trailer used to be, and watching the speed indicator through the crossing is what keeps that bounce from ever happening in the first place.

title: Retract the leveler
instruction: Retract the leveler once the trailer is unloaded and the last crossing is complete.
rationale: A leveler left extended after the last crossing is a trip hazard sitting in the doorway and a lip with nothing supporting its far end — retracting it is what returns the dock to a state the next trailer, or the next associate walking through, can actually trust.

title: Release the trailer
instruction: Release the restraint, remove the chocks, then clear the driver to pull out — in that order.
rationale: Releasing the restraint before the chocks are out risks nothing by itself, but clearing the driver before both are actually clear of the trailer is how a chock gets run over or a restraint arm gets caught as the trailer pulls away — the order exists so the last person near the wheels is always the one confirming it, not the driver guessing from the cab.

title: Sign the dock log
instruction: Sign the dock log before moving on to the next trailer.
rationale: The signed log is the record that this specific trailer, at this specific door, was actually restrained and checked before anything crossed it — not assumed fine because the last one usually is.

situation: The trailer has visibly crept forward a few centimetres away from the dock bumpers.
instruction: Stop any crossing immediately and call the driver on the dock radio — do not send the forklift across on a trailer that is moving.
missed: The creeping trailer was crossed anyway. A trailer that has already moved once with a load on the dock will move again, and the next time may be while a forklift is on the leveler.

situation: The leveler's lip has dropped and is vibrating mid-crossing — a loss of hydraulic hold.
instruction: Stop the forklift immediately and back it off the leveler. Report it to dock maintenance.
missed: The crossing continued through the drop. A leveler already losing its hold is not a leveler to finish trusting with the same load.

explanation: That gap between the trailer's rear frame and the dock bumpers means the trailer never actually backed in flush. A leveler resting its lip across a gap like that is bridging a trailer that still has room to roll before the restraint ever takes up the slack.
That dock light has been taped so it always shows green, restraint engaged or not. A light that cannot ever show red is not a safety control any more — it is a light that has been told to lie.

That restraint arm is hanging clear of the ICC bar instead of hooked under it. An arm that looks like it is in position from across the dock is not holding anything until it is actually engaged — this one is not.

That is the shortcut lever that waves a forklift across without waiting for the restraint to actually confirm. A dock light skipped once becomes a habit skipped every time, and the one trailer that was never really restrained looks exactly like every other one right up until it moves.

title: Suit up before the pre-use check
instruction: Hi-vis vest and full-body harness before touching the picker.
rationale: The harness only protects an associate who is already wearing it correctly before the platform ever leaves the ground — putting it on after the pre-use check, instead of before, is how a fitted strap gets skipped under time pressure.

title: Read the pre-use inspection tag
instruction: Confirm today's pre-use tag on the picker before stepping onto the platform.
rationale: The tag is the record that somebody already walked this specific truck today — riding the platform up without reading it means trusting a machine on nothing but how it looked from across the aisle.

title: Read the picker for what is already wrong with it
instruction: Look the picker over before stepping on. Three things are already wrong with it — find them.
rationale: A picker that looks fine from the aisle is not the same thing as one an associate has actually checked — a wedged gate, a frayed lanyard or a missing pin each quietly removes a fall-protection control, and finding them now costs a tag-out instead of costing someone the one time they needed the control that was not actually there.

title: Close the platform gate
instruction: Close the platform's own gate before the platform ever leaves the ground.
rationale: The gate is the one side of the platform rail built to open, and it only protects anyone once it is actually closed — checking it now, at ground level, is the last chance to fix it before it is a gap forty feet up.

title: Clip the lanyard to the platform anchor
instruction: Carry the lanyard's snap hook to the platform's own anchor point and clip it in before rising.
rationale: The platform's own anchor is engineered to hold a fall-arrest load; a nearby rail or a convenient loop was not — clipping to the anchor specifically, not just to something within reach, is what makes the harness a fall-arrest system instead of a costume.

title: Raise the platform to picking height
instruction: Hold the raise control until the platform reaches the marked picking height.
rationale: Holding the raise control the whole way up, rather than bumping it in short presses, is what keeps the ascent smooth and predictable — a platform that lurches in stops and starts is a platform that can catch a foot that was braced for steady motion.

title: Confirm height and load within rating
instruction: Read the height and load gauge and commit only inside the rated band.
rationale: A picker's rated capacity changes with how high the platform has gone, and the gauge is the only honest read of where this specific lift stands against that rating — reaching for one more case on the strength of how sturdy the platform feels is exactly the guess the gauge replaces.

title: Set the brakes
instruction: Set the picker's brakes before reaching out from the platform.
rationale: A picker that can creep while an associate is leaning out from the platform turns a stable reach into a moving target — setting the brakes first is what keeps the platform exactly where it was raised.

title: Pick the marked case
instruction: Select the case marked on today's pick list from the rack.
rationale: Picking the marked case rather than the nearest one is what keeps the warehouse management system's count honest — a substituted pick looks fine on this platform and shows up as a shortage three moves later, on somebody else's shift.

title: Transfer the case onto the platform
instruction: Lower the case onto the platform while keeping the load-moment indicator inside the centred band.
rationale: Watching the load-moment indicator through the transfer is what catches a case being set down off-centre before it actually tips the platform's balance — a heavy case set down blind is a platform that finds out about the imbalance only once it starts to tilt.

title: Lower the platform to the ground
instruction: Hold the lower control until the platform is fully back on the ground.
rationale: Holding the descent all the way down, the same way the ascent was held, is what keeps this from being the platform that stops half-lowered while an associate already believes it is safe to move around on.

title: Unclip the lanyard
instruction: Unclip the lanyard from the platform anchor only once the platform is fully on the ground.
rationale: The lanyard's whole job ends the moment the platform is back at ground level — unclipping any earlier, while the platform is still descending, is trading a fall-arrest connection for the belief that the descent will finish without incident.

title: Sign the pick log
instruction: Sign the pick log before moving on to the next aisle.
rationale: The signed log is the record that this specific pick, on this specific platform, actually followed the fall-protection sequence — not assumed fine because the associate usually does it right.

situation: The platform has tilted slightly to one side as the case shifted — an uneven load on the fork faces.
instruction: Stop the transfer and report the tilt to the picker radio rather than shifting your own weight to level it.
missed: The tilt was worked around instead of reported. A platform that tilts once under an uneven load will tilt again, and leaning to compensate is how an associate ends up leaning past the rail instead of behind it.

situation: An associate has walked into the aisle directly beneath the elevated platform.
instruction: Sound the horn and hold position. Do not lower the platform until the aisle is clear.
missed: The platform was lowered without sounding the horn. An aisle that was clear a moment ago is not the same thing as an aisle that is clear now.

explanation: That lanyard has a visibly frayed core strand where it runs over the snap hook — hardware that already looks like this has already taken more load than it should have. Clipping into it trades a fall-arrest device for a length of webbing that only looks like one.

That wedge block is jamming the platform gate open from the last shift's shortcut. A gate that cannot close is a gap in the one rail meant to stop a step backward from becoming a fall off the platform's own open side.

That pothole-guard pin socket is empty — the retaining pin that keeps the guard from lifting off the platform's own understructure is missing. A guard that can lift free is a guard that stops protecting the exact moment a wheel finds an uneven seam in the floor.

That is the quick-release lever that unclips the lanyard without lowering the platform first. A lanyard is only doing its job while the platform is still in the air — a lever built to remove it early removes the only thing standing between a stumble and a fall from height.

title: Suit up before approaching the cell
instruction: Hi-vis vest and hearing protection before approaching the palletizer cell.
rationale: A palletizer cell runs pneumatics and servo drives loud enough to matter over a full shift, and hearing protection is what keeps today's five-minute entry from adding up with every other cell entry this associate makes this year into a loss nobody notices until it is already permanent.

title: Read the permit-to-enter board
instruction: Confirm today's permit-to-enter before approaching the fence line.
rationale: The permit is what confirms this specific cell is actually scheduled and authorised for entry right now — approaching the fence because the arm happens to be idle is not the same thing as this cell being cleared for someone to be inside it.

title: Read the cell for what is already wrong with it
instruction: Look the cell over before approaching the gate. Three things are already wrong with it — find them.
rationale: A cell that looks routine from the fence line is not the same thing as one an associate has actually checked — a taped curtain, a defeated interlock or a covered e-stop each quietly removes a control the entry depends on, and finding them now costs a work order instead of costing someone the one time the arm was not actually done moving.

title: Request entry from the cell controller
instruction: Request entry at the cell controller before touching the gate.
rationale: Requesting entry through the controller is what tells the automation a person is about to be inside the fence, so the system holds any queued cycle instead of treating the cell as simply idle between pallets and starting the next one the moment stock arrives.

title: Isolate and lock the cell
instruction: Isolate the arm's power, apply your own lock, then apply the tag — in that order.
rationale: The isolator alone can be re-energised by anyone who does not know a person is behind the fence; the lock is what makes that impossible without that associate's own key, and the tag is what tells the next person at the panel why the lock is there — skip any one of the three and the cell is entered on a promise, not a proof.

title: Confirm zero residual energy
instruction: Read the residual motion gauge and commit only once it shows fully at zero.
rationale: Isolating the main power does not always account for stored energy in an accumulator or a counterbalance, and the gauge is the only honest read of whether the arm is actually at zero — not how still it has looked for the last minute.

title: Open the cell gate
instruction: Turn the gate latch now that the cell is isolated, locked and proven at zero energy.
rationale: Opening the gate only after every prior control is confirmed is what keeps this step from ever being the one where the cell turns out to still have something behind it that could move — a sequence run in order, not a gate opened on general confidence that the cell is probably fine by now.

title: Confirm the arm is parked safely
instruction: Confirm the arm is in its marked safe-park position before entering fully.
rationale: An arm parked outside its marked position may still be within reach of the entry path even while fully powered down — confirming its position now is what keeps the walk to the jam from ever passing closer to it than planned, isolated or not.

title: Clear the jam inside the cell
instruction: Carry the jammed pallet clear of the cell to the marked reject area.
rationale: Clearing the jam with the arm confirmed isolated, locked and parked is what makes this the routine maintenance task it should be, rather than a reach into a cell whose arm someone is trusting rather than proving, on the strength of how still it happened to look a minute ago.

title: Close the cell gate
instruction: Turn the gate latch closed and confirm it seats before releasing the isolation.
rationale: A gate that is not actually latched will not hold the interlock closed once the cell is back on power — confirming it now is what keeps the very next cycle from opening onto an unlatched fence with nobody around to notice until the arm is already moving.

title: Release the cell
instruction: Remove the tag, remove your lock, then notify the cell controller — in that order, before the arm is re-energised.
rationale: Removing the tag and the lock in the order they went on, and notifying the controller only once both are actually off, is what keeps the cell from being re-energised while anyone still believes it is locked out — reversing this order is how a restart happens on an assumption instead of a confirmation.

title: Run the proving cycle
instruction: Run the arm's slow-speed proving cycle from outside the fence, keeping its swing speed inside the safe band.
rationale: A proving cycle run at reduced speed, watched the whole way through, is what confirms the cell is actually back to normal before it goes back to full production speed — skipping straight to full speed on the assumption that the maintenance fixed everything is how a problem that was almost caught gets caught for real the hard way.

title: Sign the cell entry log
instruction: Sign the cell entry log before releasing the cell back to production.
rationale: The signed log is the record that this specific entry, on this specific cell, actually followed the permit sequence — not assumed fine because the last entry usually goes this way, and not reconstructed from memory once the shift has already moved on to the next cell.

situation: The arm has visibly settled and drifted slightly even though the isolation is confirmed — stored energy bleeding off.
instruction: Do not enter yet. Report the drift to the controls technician and have the isolation re-verified.
missed: The drift was treated as normal and entry continued. Stored energy that moves the arm once will move it again, and the second time may be with a hand already inside its reach.

situation: The cell's automation has sent a restart signal while the gate is still open.
instruction: Hit the cell's local emergency stop immediately. Do not rely on the gate interlock alone to catch this.
missed: The restart signal was left unanswered. An interlock chain that let one restart signal through while the gate was open will let the next one through too.

explanation: That light curtain sensor has tape over the lens. A curtain that cannot see anything crossing it is not stopping the arm for anything crossing it, no matter how many times someone has walked through since the tape went on without incident.
That emergency stop is covered by a stacked case. An e-stop that takes three extra seconds to reach because a box has to move first is three seconds too many the one time somebody actually needs it.

That gate interlock has been defeated with a zip tie holding the switch depressed. A gate that reads closed whether or not it actually is stops confirming anything at all — it is a formality wearing the shape of a safety device.

That is the shortcut lever that opens the gate without the permit-to-enter sequence. A cell entered once without a permit is a cell that gets entered the same way again, and the one time the arm was not actually where the last person assumed looks exactly the same from outside the fence.

title: Suit up before starting the module
instruction: Hi-vis vest and back-support belt before starting today's picks.
rationale: A back-support belt worn before the first pick, not partway through the shift once something already feels off, is what actually reinforces good lifting habits instead of arriving after the habit that needed reinforcing.

title: Read the rotation schedule
instruction: Confirm today's job-rotation schedule before starting the module.
rationale: The rotation schedule is what keeps this module from being the only thing an associate's body does for an entire shift — reading it now is what makes the rotation something planned for, not something skipped when the pick count is going well.

title: Read the module for what is already wrong with it
instruction: Look the module over before starting. Three things are already wrong with it — find them.
rationale: A module that looks routine at the start of a shift is not the same thing as one an associate has actually checked — an overhead overweight case, a stuck light or a missing guard each quietly turns an ordinary pick into the one that goes wrong, and finding them now costs a report instead of costing someone a strain or a caught hand.

title: Confirm the pick quantity
instruction: Confirm the display's quantity before reaching for the lit bin.
rationale: The display is what actually says how many to pick — the light only says which bin, and trusting the light alone is how a quantity gets picked wrong even when the bin was exactly right.

title: Pick from the lit bin
instruction: Pick from the bin the light and the display both point to.
rationale: Picking from the bin both signals agree on, rather than the one that is simply closest, is what keeps the warehouse management system's count accurate for whoever pulls from this module next.

title: Lower the lift-assist table
instruction: Turn the lift-assist crank to bring the heavy case down to waist height before lifting it.
rationale: Bringing the case to waist height with the lift-assist, rather than reaching up or bending down to where it sits, is what keeps this lift inside the posture range a back can repeat all shift without accumulating the strain the awkward version of the same lift would.

title: Advance the tote
instruction: Hold the advance button until the tote reaches the pack station.
rationale: Holding the advance the whole way, rather than bumping it and walking away, is what keeps the tote from stopping short at a point on the lane it was never meant to sit — exactly where the next associate would have to reach further than planned to reach it.

title: Confirm the pick pace
instruction: Read the pace gauge and commit only within the sustainable band.
rationale: The pace gauge is the only honest read of whether this rate is sustainable for a full shift — matching whatever the system asks for, rather than what the gauge shows as sustainable, is exactly how a pace that feels fine for an hour stops feeling fine by the end of a shift.

title: Carry the case to the tote
instruction: Carry the picked case to the waiting tote.
rationale: Carrying the case close to the body for the short distance to the tote, rather than swinging it out at arm's length, is what keeps even a light case from loading the lower back the way an extended reach would.

title: Load the tote lane
instruction: Load the tote onto the lane while keeping the lane speed indicator inside the safe band.
rationale: Watching the lane speed while loading is what keeps a tote from being set down onto a lane running too fast to receive it gently — a tote dropped onto a fast lane is a tote that can bounce back into the hand that just set it down.

title: Take the scheduled stretch break
instruction: Run both stretches on the posted guide before the next cycle.
rationale: A stretch break taken on schedule, rather than skipped because the pick count is going well, is what the site's own ergonomics programme is actually counting on to offset a shift's worth of the same repeated motion.

title: Rotate to the next task
instruction: Move to the next task on the rotation schedule.
rationale: Taking the rotation for real, rather than treating the schedule as a suggestion, is what actually varies the muscles and joints this shift asks something of — the whole point of a rotation is a body that is not doing the exact same motion for the exact same eight hours.

title: Sign the rotation log
instruction: Sign the rotation log before leaving the module.
rationale: The signed log is the record that this specific rotation was actually taken — not assumed fine because the schedule says it should have been.

situation: The system's demanded pick rate has spiked well above the sustainable pace.
instruction: Signal the shift lead rather than matching the system's demanded pace.
missed: The pace spike was matched instead of reported. A pace held past what is sustainable for one spike gets asked for again the next time the system sees it worked once.

situation: An overloaded neighbouring bin has visibly shifted and is tipping forward slightly.
instruction: Stop and report the tipping shelf to the shift lead rather than pushing it back into place by hand.
missed: The tipping shelf was pushed back into place instead of reported. A shelf that tips once under an overload will tip again unless the overload is actually addressed.

explanation: That tote-lane guard has been removed from over the drive roller. A guard missing from a moving lane is a pinch point sitting in reach of anyone loading a tote, whether or not it has caught anyone yet.

That case is marked overweight and stacked above shoulder height. Reaching overhead for a case heavier than the rest is exactly the combination — height plus load — that turns an ordinary pick into the rep that actually hurts a shoulder.

That sign reads 'skip rotation, stay on pick' taped over the rotation schedule. Skipping the scheduled rotation to keep the count up trades a short-term pace gain for exactly the kind of repetitive strain the rotation schedule exists to prevent.

That pick light has stuck on, lit over a bin nobody actually queued a pick from. A light trusted on its own, without checking the display's quantity against it, sends a pick from the wrong bin exactly as confidently as it sends one from the right one.

title: Read the incoming job
instruction: Read the job card: which agent asked, the task, the site, the speed and the policy.
rationale: Every job that arrives from a software agent starts as a request, not an order, and the job card is where it says who is asking and for what; a supervisor who reads it first can match the request to the site, the task to the allowlist and the policy to its lineage before anything is allowed to move.

title: Check who asked
instruction: Find the client agent in the site's agent registry and read what it is allowed to request.
rationale: An agent that is not in the registry has no history anyone can audit and no list of tasks it may ask for, so its job is refused before any detail is weighed; checking the registry is the same step as checking a contractor's sign-in sheet before letting them near a machine.

title: Find the job that is not on the allowlist
instruction: Find the queued job asking for a task that is not on the allowlist.
rationale: An allowlist means a task is refused unless it was reviewed and written down beforehand, which is the opposite of trusting a request because it sounds routine; a job asking to bypass a safeguard is exactly the kind a software agent might generate from a badly worded goal, and it never reaches the robot.

title: Read the policy's eval card
instruction: Read the eval card: held-out results against the random baseline and the scripted expert, and the violations.
rationale: The policy that will drive the simulated robot has to show what it does on seeds it never saw, measured against a floor and a ceiling, with its safe-practice violations counted beside its successes; an agent's job that names a policy with no eval card, or only a success figure, is not ready to run.

title: Find the stale policy
instruction: Find the policy trained on revoked demonstrations.
rationale: Revoking consent deletes the recordings, but a policy trained on them still carries what it copied, so the lineage board marks it stale and the governor refuses it; catching the stale policy is how a person's withdrawn consent actually reaches the robot an agent wants to run.

title: Set the speed limit from the risk assessment
instruction: Set the governor's speed limit to the value in the site's risk assessment and commit when it matches.
rationale: The speed a job may ask for is capped by the site's written risk assessment, not by what the agent requests or what the robot can do; setting the cap from the sheet before the job runs means a request above it is refused by rule, and the supervisor never has to argue a number with software in the moment.

title: Walk the governor's checks in order
instruction: Check the e-stop status, then the allowlist, then speed and separation, then the policy lineage.
rationale: The governor checks the e-stop first because a held stop overrides every other answer: there is no task, speed or policy that makes it right to move a robot someone has stopped; walking the checks in the same order the software does is how a supervisor learns to read its refusals.

title: Confirm the physical path is locked off
instruction: Confirm the physical-robot switch is locked off and names a human approver.
rationale: A command that starts with a software agent reaches only the simulated robot here; sending one to a real arm would need a named human approver at the site on top of every governor rule, and that path ships disabled, so the supervisor confirms the lock rather than assuming it.

title: Approve the job for the sim, under your name
instruction: Approve the job for the simulated robot under your own name.
rationale: Approval moves the job from negotiation to the work phase and is written into the audit log with the supervisor's name, so responsibility for letting software drive a robot, even a simulated one, sits with a person who read the evidence rather than with the agent that asked.

title: Watch the run from outside the zone
instruction: Hold at the watch point outside the zone while the simulated run starts.
rationale: A run dispatched by an agent is watched by a person who can stop it, from a place the robot cannot reach; the governor checks every step, but only the supervisor can see that a move is wrong for a reason no rule anticipated.

title: Keep the separation in band
instruction: Keep the separation readout in its band while the run continues at reduced speed.
rationale: Inside the warning distance the robot runs at the reduced speed and inside the stop distance it holds a protective stop; tracking the separation readout keeps the supervisor's attention on the person and the robot rather than on the job's progress bar.

title: File the evaluation
instruction: Carry the evaluation memo to the job's evaluation slot: completed, or rejected with the reason.
rationale: The evaluation closes the job: completed only if the run finished with every safe practice kept and no stop, rejected otherwise with the reason in plain words; filing it is how the client agent, the site and the next reviewer learn what happened rather than what was hoped.

title: Check the audit chain
instruction: Check the audit log: every allow, refuse and stop is there and the chain is intact.
rationale: Each audit line carries a hash of the line before it, so a missing or edited decision breaks the chain where anyone can see it; checking it at the end of a job confirms that the record of who asked, what the governor decided and who approved will still be there when someone needs it.

situation: The simulated arm has turned off its planned path toward the teammate's keep-out zone on the bench.
instruction: Press the run e-stop now.
missed: The run went on after the arm turned toward the keep-out zone. The e-stop wins: stop first, investigate second.

situation: The client agent has re-sent the same job asking for full speed with a person inside the warning distance.
instruction: Refuse the re-sent job.
missed: The faster re-send sat in the queue unanswered. Refuse it: inside the warning distance only the reduced speed is allowed.

explanation: That switches the queue to approve every job from this agent automatically. A software agent can be wrong, out of date or misconfigured, and it cannot see the person walking into the cell; the human review of each job is the safeguard the agent does not have.

That clears the audit log to tidy the screen. The log is append-only on purpose: every allow, refuse and stop is chained to the line before it, so anyone can later see which agent asked for what and who decided, and a cleared log hides exactly what a review needs.

That walks onto the taped floor beside the bench to get a closer look at the simulated run. A dispatcher keeps the same footing a technician would on live equipment, because habits built at a sim desk follow people onto real floors, and nobody predicts a policy's next move from inches away.

That routes the job to the physical cell. A command that starts with a software agent reaches only the simulated robot in this setup; driving a real arm would need a named human approver at the site, and that path is locked off by design.
